==English== {{wp}} {{wikiquote}} ===Alternative forms=== * {{alt|en|risque||archaic}} ===Etymology=== {{etymon|en|:from|risque|tree=1}} From earlier {{m|en|risque}}, from {{bor|en|frm|risque}}, from {{der|en|roa-oit|risco|t=risk}} (modern {{cog|it|rischio}}) and {{m|it|rischiare|t=to run into danger}}. Displaced native {{cog|ang|pleoh||risk}} and {{m|ang|plēon||to risk}}. {{col-top|2|Speculation on earlier roots}} Most dictionaries consider the etymology of these Italian terms {{unc|en|nocap=1}}, but some suggest they perhaps come from {{der|en|la-vul|*resecum||that which cuts, rock, crag}} (> {{cog|la-med|resicu}}), from {{der|en|la|resecō||cut off, loose, curtail|pos=verb}}, in the sense of that which is a danger to boating or shipping; or from {{der|en|grc|ῥιζικόν||root, radical, hazard}}. A few dictionaries express more certainty. Collins says the {{der|en|it|risco}} comes from {{der|en|grc|ῥίζα||cliff}} due to the hazards of sailing along rocky coasts. The American Heritage says it probably comes from {{der|en|gkm|ῥιζικό|ῥιζικό, ριζικό|t=sustenance obtained by a soldier through his own initiative, fortune}}, from {{der|en|ar|رِزْق|t=sustenance, that which God allots}}, from {{der|en|syc|ܪܙܩܐ|ܪܘܙܝܩܐ ,ܪܙܩܐ|tr=rezqā, rōzīqā|t=daily ration}}, from {{der|en|pal|tr=rōzīg}} (whence {{cog|fa-cls|روزِی}}), from {{der|en|pal|tr=rōz|t=day}} (whence {{cog|fa-cls|روز}}), from {{der|en|peo|𐎼𐎢𐎨𐏃|tr=raučah}} (cognate with {{cog|sa|रोचस्|t=[[light]], [[lustre]]}}), from {{der|en|ira-pro|*ráwčah}}, from {{der|en|iir-pro|*ráwčas}}, ultimately from {{der|en|ine-pro|*léwkos|*léwk-os}}, from {{suf|ine-pro|*lewk-|t1=bright; to shine|*-os|pos2=noun suffix|nocat=1}}. Karla Mallette derives the word from {{der|en|ar|رِزْق|t=sustenance, that which God allots}} via {{bor|en|pml|-}}.{{cite-web |title=Mediterranean lingua franca, ca. 1450-1650: Threshold or holdover? |url=https://studyingteachingthemediterranean.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/karla-mallette-lingua-franca.pdf |accessdate=4 September 2025 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20250813071833/https://studyingteachingthemediterranean.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/karla-mallette-lingua-franca.pdf|archivedate=13 August 2025}} Cognate with {{cog|es|riesgo}}, {{cog|pt|risco}} {{col-bottom}} ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/ɹɪsk/}} * {{audio|en|En-us-risk.ogg|a=US}} * {{homophones|en|RISC|risque}} {{qualifier|rare dialect}} * {{rhymes|en|ɪsk|s=1}} ===Noun=== {{en-noun|~}} # {{lb|en|uncountable}} The [[probability]] of a negative outcome to a decision or event. #: {{ux|en|There is '''risk''' of being brutalized, arrested, imprisoned and tortured, all because I want you to know the truth about this matter.}} #* {{quote-book|en|title=On-farm Reservoir Systems for Rainfed Ricelands| page=36| url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=9712200663| author=S. I. Bhuiyan| year=1994| passage=What crop(s) to plant, how much area to devote to each crop, and how much '''risk''' to take with respect to rainfall during the season are some of the decisions that must be made.}} #* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-06-22| volume=407| issue=8841| page=76| title=[http://www.economist.com/news/books-and-arts/21579801-making-sense-statistics-riddle-our-days-snakes-and-ladders Snakes and ladders]| passage='''Risk''' is everywhere. From tabloid headlines insisting that coffee causes cancer (yesterday, of course, it cured it) to stern government warnings about alcohol and driving, the world is teeming with goblins. For each one there is a frighteningly precise measurement of just how likely it is to jump from the shadows and get you.
Taking regular exercise, coupled with a healthy diet, reduced the '''risk''' of several types of cancer.}} # {{lb|en|uncountable}} The magnitude of possible loss consequent to a decision or event. # {{lb|en|uncountable|economics|business|and|engineering}} The [[potential]] [[negative]] [[effect#Noun|effect]] of an [[event]], determined by [[multiplying]] the [[likelihood]] of the event occurring with its [[magnitude]] should it [[occur]]. # {{lb|en|countable}} A [[possible]] [[adverse]] [[event]] or [[outcome]]. #: {{synonyms|en|danger|peril|hazard}} ## {{lb|en|insurance}} A type of adverse [[event]] covered under an insurance policy. #* {{RQ:Macaulay History of England|chapter=7|passage=the imminent and constant '''risk''' of assassination, a risk which has shaken very strong nerves}} # {{lb|en|countable}} A [[thing]] (from the perspective of how likely or unlikely it is to cause an adverse effect). #: {{ux|en|That man is going to be a big '''risk''' once he's out of prison.}} #: {{ux|en|Those stairs are a major '''risk'''.}} ## {{lb|en|banking|finance}} A [[borrower]] (such as a [[mortgage]]-holder or person with a [[credit card]]). ##: {{ux|en|A good credit rating indicates the customer is a desirable '''risk'''.}} ## {{lb|en|finance}} A [[financial]] [[product]] (typically an [[investment]]). ##: {{ux|en|Subprime mortgages are poor '''risks'''; especially for a pension scheme.}} ## {{lb|en|insurance}} An [[entity]] [[insure]]d by an [[insurer]]. ====Usage notes==== * When referring to some possible cause of an adverse effect as "a risk", the default position is that one is referring to how likely it is to cause an adverse effect. Such use is qualified with adjectives that refer to magnitude, such as "major", "large" or "tiny". However, adjectives that refer to quality (such as "good" or "undesirable") indicate that one is referring to how unlikely the adverse effect is, and this usage is invariably restricted to monetary contexts. On the other hand, the former sense may be used in any context (including monetary risks). In academic finance, risk is associated with the variance of the expected outcome, and not with the probability of outcomes (see Black-Scholes) ====Hyponyms==== * {{sense|formal business and
